prompt: A manager says, “The detector catches almost every attack, so almost every alert must be an attack.” Which missing comparison most directly exposes the base-rate mistake?

options.text: Whether the detector runs on separate machines.
options.explanation: Physical separation does not address the reversed conditional probability.

options.text: Whether the observed sequence alternated alerts and quiet periods.
options.explanation: That sequence pattern does not supply the missing prevalence comparison.

options.text: Whether the test metric is expressed as a percentage.
options.explanation: Changing notation does not restore the omitted prior.

options.text: True alerts versus false alerts after accounting for how common attacks are.
options.explanation: Many benign cases can produce more false alerts even at a low false-positive rate.

workedExample: The manager starts with attacks and then draws a conclusion about alerts. Rebuild the alert population from attacked and benign cases, using each group’s size and flag rate.

link.title: Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell

prompt: A fraud team receives many false alerts because legitimate payments vastly outnumber fraud. Holding sensitivity and prevalence fixed, which change directly improves alert precision?

options.text: Duplicate every alert in the queue.
options.explanation: Both true and false alerts are duplicated; no new evidence is created.

options.text: Ignore how common legitimate payments are.
options.explanation: That removes information needed to interpret alerts.
This removes false alerts while preserving expected true detections under the premise.
Changing a label does not change the alert population.

workedExample: Precision concerns the composition of alerts. Under fixed sensitivity, true detections stay the same; reducing false positives leaves a larger true share. A real threshold change may alter sensitivity too and must be measured.

prompt: An intrusion detector has high classifier recall but its alert queue is dominated by false positives. Which interpretations are justified? Select all that apply.

options.text: Every individual alert can safely be dismissed.
options.explanation: An aggregate composition does not establish that a particular alert is false.

options.text: It may still be useful evidence that an attack occurred.
options.explanation: A flag may raise attack probability while leaving it below one-half.

options.text: High sensitivity alone does not establish high precision.
options.explanation: Sensitivity starts from real attacks; precision starts from alerts.

options.text: Changing the screened population requires checking conditional detector rates again.
options.explanation: Selection may alter sensitivity and false-positive rate as well as prevalence.

workedExample: Distinguish whether the detector catches attacks from whether its alerts are usually attacks. Then separate model-average queue composition from decisions about an individual case with additional evidence.
